newsitem.title: USA: Emerging markets debt mixed in slow trade Monday.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets debt mixed in slow trade Monday.

text.p: Emerging market debt traded mixed on Monday, with many issues moving lower in sympathy with U.S. Treasuries, traders said.
"Things are quiet but doing well," one trader said. "We lost a little ground this morning, but things have held up since then."

Early in the session, expansionary U.S. economic reports pointed the market lower, traders said. The Chicagoland Business Barometer rose to 61.5 in June from 56.8 in May, and new home sales grew to an annual rate of 825,000 last month from 770,000 the month before.
Ecuador debt tallied the day's greatest losses as investors awaited word on the future of the country's financial leadership. PDIs ECPDI=RR were off 3/8 at 64-5/8 in late trading.
Finance Minister Carlos Davalos tendered his resignation last week, but President Fabian Alarcon had not yet announced whether he would accept his withdrawal.
"We're still waiting to hear who has resigned and if other resignations will happen," one trader said. "The bonds have widened out, and we would expect that to continue."
But other traders said buyers began to step back into Ecuador on Monday, perhaps betting that central bank head Fidel Jaramillo would remain in office.
"We've seen small Ecuadorean accounts buying in at these levels," another trader said. "It doesn't look like the governor of the central bank will be replaced or resign."
Among major Latin America issues, Brazil "C" BR8D14=RR were off 3/8 at 80-3/8, Argentina FRBs ARFLC05 were up 1/4 at 94 and Mexico pars MX625L19=RR were off 1/4 at 77-1/4.
Looking ahead, investors are focused on Thursday's U.S. employment report rather than the two-day Federal Reserve policy meeting that begins Tuesday, traders said.
Wall Street economists in a Reuters poll unanimously projected no rate shift at the July 1-2 Federal Open market Committee Meeting.

June payrolls, however, are seen as an important indicator of what the Fed might do at its next meeting, in August. On average, economists forecast an addition of 222,000 to payrolls this month, compared with 138,000 in May.
